# Synthesis and research agenda {#sec-synthesis-agenda}

District assistance, hospital ratings and employer report cards communicate conclusions drawn from imperfect evidence. The decisions they inform differ, however: eligibility, comparative reporting, selection and intervention each impose particular requirements. In @sec-public-decisions we asked which comparisons to communicate, how they can be wrong and what further judgment is needed before acting on them.

We have formulated the choice of common grades as a mathematical decision problem. The grades form an ordered partition: different grades disclose a direction, while a common grade withholds one. The problem specifies the targets, their uncertainty, the costs of errors and withholding, and the permissible reports. Assessing measurement validity, adopting institutional preferences and establishing improvements in public outcomes require further evidence and judgment.

The results and illustrations identify circumstances in which common grades may be useful and specify the comparisons covered by their guarantees. Comparison with the literature also identifies objectives for which other procedures may be preferable. A common report can serve its intended purpose without dominating every conventional rule.

## The two reporting targets {#sec-synthesis-targets}

The first choice concerns the meaning of a correct direction. A scalar composite combines criterion magnitudes on declared scales, with coefficients $a$ specifying their contributions to the target. A criterion-direction objective evaluates errors separately on each criterion and weights them by $w$. These objectives can assign different costs to the same report even when all target values are known, so their disagreement need not arise from estimation error. We therefore retain both as co-primary targets, as defined in @sec-target-definitions and @sec-two-estimands.

Measurement and valuation must therefore be specified before optimization. The indicators may measure a common construct or represent distinct concerns; precise evidence or a fitted association alone cannot establish which interpretation is appropriate. Nor do equal coefficients necessarily express neutral tradeoffs. In decision analysis, coefficients are interpreted in relation to attributes, scales and elicited comparisons, and an additive representation requires more than the presence of several attributes [@keeney_raiffa_1993, pp. 66–69, 116–123]. Here directional-error weights value mistakes in the report. Interpreting them as utility coefficients for institutional outcomes would require additional justification.

The targets also have different invariance properties. Common strictly increasing transformations within criteria preserve directional-error events if the joint law is transported accordingly and the report domain is retained. They need not preserve the ordering of a fixed cardinal composite. The scalar composite thus addresses a distinct question and need not be interpreted as an approximation to the directional objective. Evaluating both targets, together with their agreement conditions, distinguishes improved performance from a change in the definition of success.

## Relation to earlier work {#sec-synthesis-inheritance}

The analysis follows posterior decision theory. Bayesian ranking distinguishes parameter estimation, rank estimation and selection of leading units under application-specific losses [@laird1989ranking, pp. 31–33; @lin2006ranking, pp. 916–920; @henderson2016cut, pp. 783–788]. These purposes must be chosen in addition to specifying a posterior distribution. Kline, Rose, and Walters provide the direct report-card foundation by choosing coherent scalar grades under supplied beliefs and a tradeoff between correct and incorrect comparisons [@kline_discrimination_2024, pp. 2477–2482]. In @sec-scalar-reduction we express that scalar principle using the normalization and withholding convention adopted here.

We extend the scalar construction to a weighted directional loss for several criteria. Finite linearity of expectation gives the pair-coefficient identity, and the whole-criterion mixture gives a further connection to the scalar problem, subject to the equality correction and common-domain conditions in @sec-criterion-mixture. These results characterize the information and assumptions required for this objective; they are not claims of priority for weighted ranking or a general social-choice representation. The audience interpretation requires additional behavioral assumptions and describes averaged pairwise choices, rather than welfare from allocating across all units.

Other literatures address related but distinct decisions. Rank confidence sets and joint posterior ordering statements protect events that differ from expected wrong-direction counts. Partial-order methods preserve structural incomparability; preference aggregation summarizes supplied judgments; multicriteria acceptability examines modeled valuations; and sorting assigns predefined classes or purchases further judgments. As discussed in @sec-uncertainty-ordering and @sec-aggregation-mcda, converting these outputs into common grades can change the decision problem. Their metric properties, approximation factors, reconstruction bounds and coverage guarantees remain conditional on the original formulations, even when the outputs share pairwise notation or tied groups.

The compound-decision debate further illustrates the need to specify the error criterion and probability law separately. The Gu–Koenker reply gives a fixed-sequence interpretation of a componentwise average-risk calculation, while the comments distinguish this calculation from protection at particular parameter configurations [@gu2023reply, pp. 61–62; @mogstad2023comment, pp. 54–57]. A Bayesian or frequentist label alone does not capture that distinction. Neither argument directly establishes properties of coupled grade actions; those properties require the reporting formulation and assumptions used here.

## Consequences of the reporting problem {#sec-synthesis-established}

Requiring coherence restricts the action family independently of the probability distribution. Individually preferred pair decisions may be incompatible with an ordered partition. Within-grade silence must form equivalence classes in the report, although it asserts no equality of the targets. The counts in @sec-grade-actions describe how many comparisons a report discloses, and the examples in @sec-pair-versus-grade show that a pairwise relaxation need not be attainable by common grades. Further restricting the grade count or fixing the order can introduce additional loss.

Expected risk under the additive directional objective is determined by within-criterion pair probabilities, without requiring independence across criteria. Scalar-composite ordering and simultaneous correctness can require joint information that these coefficients do not supply. The constructions in @sec-weighted-directional-risk and @sec-two-estimands illustrate this difference while allowing latent equality. In particular, forward and reverse error probabilities need not be complementary.

Criterion protections remove reports from the feasible family, while preference sensitivity changes their relative objective values. For a fixed report with positive disclosure, an expected-count constraint has the stated expected-fraction interpretation under the supplied law. At zero disclosure the count inequality remains defined but the fraction does not, and feasibility of all-tie still depends on the domain. Expected-criterion minimax instead minimizes the largest included expected criterion loss, which differs from taking the expectation of a statewise maximum. The protection and withholding results in @sec-protections-preferences retain these distinctions and their associated conditions.

We give two computational representations. Binary total-preorder variables represent unrestricted grades; dynamic programming gives an exact segmentation of a fixed order for the stated additive objective. The latter guarantee applies within that restricted family and does not automatically extend to protected or minimax problems. The certificates in @sec-solver-qualifications require a feasible report and valid bounds for the specified domain. We then distinguish coefficient approximation from optimization error and show how coefficient errors affect protection feasibility. Concentration results require their stated sampling assumptions; an effective sample size diagnostic alone cannot supply a finite-sample certificate. These results justify the specified calculations under their assumptions, leaving the reliability of a fitted procedure for further assessment.

## Evaluation and competing objectives {#sec-synthesis-evaluation}

An exact Bayes action has expected loss no greater than that of any eligible comparator under the same law and objective. This comparison also holds under $P$ when the relevant selection and conditional evaluation risks agree, subject to the stated feasibility and integrability conditions. The conditional results in @sec-conditional-bayes-dominance therefore determine the direction of some comparisons before an experiment is run. They do not determine the size of the advantage, justify the loss, establish performance under another law, objective or domain, or demonstrate an institutional improvement.

Because withholding alone can reduce the wrong count, disclosure must accompany the comparison. Equal grade counts need not give equal numbers $N$ of disclosed pairs: the group sizes also matter. For a specified finite family and law, the frontier in @sec-matched-disclosure-frontier compares expected wrong counts at matched expected disclosure, allowing randomization over complete reports at some operating points. A sparse candidate path can miss frontier points, and an approximate frontier retains its approximation qualifications. The choice of error summary matters as well. A pooled count ratio generally differs from an average of dataset-specific fractions, and a report with no disclosures supplies no evidence of perfect comparative accuracy under either convention.

For allocation, the relevant benchmarks depend on the utility. Under the stated exact-budget and utility conditions, posterior means maximize expected additive selected value, while latent top-set membership probabilities maximize expected overlap with that set. A grade-based lottery adds a selection rule and may attain neither optimum. Absolute-threshold classification and stability under repeated information introduce further objectives. The contrasts in @sec-selection-benchmarks and @sec-objective-precision-contrast quantify the resulting costs: a report useful for public communication can be less useful for selecting recipients under a particular budget.

Interpreting an error summary requires identifying both the selection beliefs $\Pi_s$ and the evaluation law $P$. Conditional self-consistency under the supplied model does not establish external calibration. Misspecification may leave some decisions unchanged, and self-reported errors may be optimistic, pessimistic or accurate. The bounds in @sec-model-error-bound describe the consequences of a specified discrepancy without estimating it in an application. More precise numerical calculations cannot resolve that model discrepancy or justify the institutional values adopted in the loss.

## The prospective P1 study {#sec-synthesis-p1-study}

P1 will compare the errors communicated by specified common rules with those under posterior grading at comparable disclosure, together with costs under competing objectives. The questions in @sec-p1-evaluation-bridge concern total differences, their descriptive decomposition, variation across settings, competing objectives and calibration of reported errors. This empirical study remains to be carried out. Known-posterior optimality and the present illustrations do not determine its results.

The exact finite examples show how the two targets can select different reports, how a mean ordering can differ from that preferred under directional reporting loss, and why disclosure and subsequent selection require separate evaluation. The historical KRW illustration instead evaluates two reconstructed common-grade actions using retained signed-target inputs and the historical coefficient convention. Recovery of the archived summaries supports consistency for those actions and inputs. It leaves the original posterior producer, execution environment and common-grade frontier unverified, and the retained pair arrays do not identify the probabilities for a cardinal race–gender composite (@sec-krw-reuse-interpretation).

The planned study evaluates each rule against both co-primary targets, retaining its actual information and action restrictions and distinguishing exact optima from candidate solutions. Varying signal, precision, dependence, target construction and model specification can identify conditions under which the comparison changes. Descriptive factor decompositions allocate a defined contrast among operations without identifying causal effects of estimation or grade boundaries. Allocation, classification, stability and criterion-specific errors provide additional evaluations. Small or absent gains, reversals under another law and costs under the alternatives' native objectives all contribute to answering these questions, so the study need not find an advantage for posterior grading.

Inherited foundations, qualified derivations, software scope, bounded illustrations and the prospective P1 study. Posterior decision and ranking principles and KRW’s coherent scalar report-card problem are inherited foundations. The monograph adapts that foundation and develops qualified results for common reports, coefficient information, feasible domains and evaluation. Documented software implements specified routes rather than every result, and its equality-neutral scope remains deliberately narrower. Exact finite examples and two archived KRW action reconstructions provide bounded illustrations. P1’s comparisons, magnitudes, setting dependence, competing-objective costs and calibration remain prospective. The two co-primary target definitions and the conditions attached to each result govern these conclusions.

## Further research {#sec-synthesis-open-agenda}

One extension would change the interpretation of ties. Under weak-error loss, a strict disclosure at latent equality is wrong and a reported tie withholds a direction. A practical-equivalence band would define new target events and a new loss, potentially permitting a positive equivalence assertion. It would require substantive margins, an uncertainty statement for those events and a coherent action definition. It therefore addresses a further question rather than an equality case omitted from the present formulation.

The equality-neutral branch in @sec-tie-aware-loss retains exact equality and assigns it zero directional and withholding cost. It consequently changes the all-withhold baseline and the disclosure quantity, without introducing a practical-equivalence band. Weak-error loss remains appropriate when a strict assertion at equality is to count as wrong. Choosing between these conventions requires specifying what constitutes an erroneous comparison and a withheld opportunity. The software described in @sec-package-tie-aware implements a narrower equality-neutral problem; the historical route's protections, diagnostics and numerical guarantees do not all extend to that implementation.

Further work could compare action families. Partial orders, selected comparisons, separate criterion cards and predefined classes can retain information that a common ordered partition reorganizes or suppresses. Their usefulness depends on the institutional purpose and the meaning of silence. Comparing representation costs while retaining each family's native guarantees would require a broader analysis. Likewise, studying the costs of criterion protections requires explicit objectives and feasible domains. The present examples and family-inclusion arguments establish neither general representation-cost nor protection-cost theorems, and aggregation guarantees continue to require their original assumptions.

Uncertainty about one person's preferences, disagreement among people and an analyst's sensitivity distribution over weights require different interpretations. Fixed-weight and expected-minimax analyses compare reports under specified preferences; they do not identify legitimate public preferences. An extension would need to identify who supplies valuations, the evidence informing them, any dependence with uncertain outcomes and the authority adopting the report. The methods in @sec-mcda-acceptability-sorting and recommendations in @sec-governance-preferences offer starting points. Sampling repeatedly from a uniform weight distribution supplies no evidence of population preferences.

Each extension brings computational and inferential requirements. Algorithms for larger report families or additional constraints need approximation and feasibility guarantees for those problems. Model development must address the target population, dependence, hyperparameter uncertainty and the relation between precision and the reported quantity. Better integration or tighter solver bounds can improve calculations under supplied beliefs but leave empirical calibration to be assessed. Their practical value therefore depends on the report and its use.

Allocation based on intervention benefit requires a causal target. High measured need, severe disparity or reliably higher priority does not establish that a unit would improve most under a particular intervention. The analysis must specify the intervention, feasible recipients and resources, valued consequences and assumptions supporting a causal interpretation. A grade can inform this analysis but supplies neither the causal estimand nor evidence of benefit. These governance choices enter the formulation before optimization.

Common grades provide a way to communicate selected comparisons with their targets, uncertainty, values and limitations. Their adoption depends on the intended decision and the available alternatives. The present analysis supplies a formal and interpretive basis for that assessment. P1's empirical comparisons, including unfavorable findings, will help identify when common grades are useful and when another action better serves the institutional purpose.
